title: "4. Small-signal AC"
subtitle: "Compute gain and phase versus frequency"

  env: ["JULIA_PROJECT=../../.."]

```{julia}
#| include: false
using Pkg
Pkg.activate("../..")
using Amber
```

Small-signal analysis linearizes the circuit about its DC operating point and
solves it over a frequency grid. The source's `ac` value supplies the phasor
excitation; its transient waveform is unrelated.

```{julia}
@circuit RCLowPass(; R=10kΩ, C=10nF) begin
    gnd = ground()
    input = node()
    output = node()
    Source = voltage_source(input, gnd; dc=0V, ac=1V)
    R1 = resistor(input, output; value=R)
    C1 = capacitor(output, gnd; value=C)
    observe(voltage(input), voltage(output))
end

circuit = RCLowPass();
response = small_signal(
    circuit,
    10Hz => 1MHz;
    source=:Source,
    points=301,
    scale=:log,
);
```

## Complex results first

AC voltages are complex phasors. Preserve the complex response until you know
which representation you need.

```{julia}
frequency = frequencies(response)
gain = transfer(
    response;
    input=voltage(:input),
    output=voltage(:output),
)

gain_db = db20.(magnitude(gain))
phase_deg = phase(gain; unwrap=true, degrees=true);
```

The ideal corner is $f_c=1/(2\pi RC)$ and the gain there is about
$-3.01\,\mathrm{dB}$.

```{julia}
corner = inv(2π * 10kΩ * 10nF)
index = argmin(abs.(frequency .- corner))

(frequency=frequency[index], gain_db=gain_db[index], phase_deg=phase_deg[index])
```

The explicit `source=:Source` becomes important when a circuit contains more
than one independent source. It makes the experiment unambiguous and
reproducible.

::: {.callout-note}
AC analysis predicts infinitesimal behavior around the bias point. Use a
transient simulation to study clipping, slew rate, switching, and other
large-signal effects.
:::
